messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 34
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: School Counselor
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 77

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Stress: Stress, Medical Procedures: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure, Olfactory (Smell): Related smells
  Maladaptive Strategies: Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time, Avoid Police: Police, Avoid Thinking: Thinking about the event
  Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
  Memory: Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing, Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

David, a 34-year-old school counselor, traces the fracture in his life back to a Saturday afternoon nine months ago. He was helping his neighbour, Mark, build a deck. David was on the circular saw when it happened—a kickback on a piece of pressure-treated lumber. The saw leapt from his hands, and in a fraction of a second that now stretches into an eternity, it struck Mark’s teenage son, Leo, who had been standing nearby. The event itself is a blur of disconnected sensory fragments: the high-pitched scream of the motor, the jolt in his arms, the coppery smell of blood mixing with sawdust, and the sight of Leo on the ground. The police who responded were kind, but their questions felt like accusations, cementing a nascent, horrifying thought: this was his fault.

In the weeks that followed, the memory began to intrude. It was never a simple recollection; it was a full-body re-experiencing. When the memory came, it felt like it was happening right now, not something that was over. He would be sitting in his office at school and suddenly feel the weight of the saw in his hands, his heart hammering in his chest as if he were back in the yard. This terrifying sense of presence, the feeling of being trapped in that moment, brought with it waves of guilt and horror so profound they left him breathless. Each time the memory ambushed him, it reinforced the devastating conclusion he had drawn: the accident happened because of the way he acted, a direct result of his carelessness. He felt he could no longer trust himself to do the right thing.

Soon, the world became a landscape of hidden threats. The smell of cut wood from a nearby construction site would instantly throw him back into the memory, and he began taking longer routes to work to avoid it. This was the start of a pattern. Encountering a trigger, like the high-pitched whine of a vacuum cleaner, would immediately bring the memory crashing back, complete with the sensory details and the crushing self-blame. To manage this, he started to keep his mind occupied at all times, a constant barrage of podcasts and news radio from the moment he woke until he fell into a fitful sleep. He believed that if he could just keep his brain busy enough, he could outrun the thoughts. But the more he tried to deliberately avoid thinking about the event, the more violently the memories would intrude when his guard inevitably dropped.

This conviction that he was fundamentally flawed and untrustworthy became the organizing principle of his life. His self-blame made him hypervigilant, constantly scanning for anything that might remind him of his failure, which only made him more likely to find it. This core belief drove his avoidance; he reasoned that a person as dangerously incompetent as him needed to be contained. He stopped offering to help friends with household projects and began finding excuses to avoid parent-teacher meetings at work where conflict might arise, certain he would give the wrong advice. The sheer effort of this constant mental distraction left him perpetually exhausted and on edge, which in turn made the memories feel even closer and more threatening. His failure to engage with the world as he once had only served as further proof to him that his life had been destroyed by the trauma.

His work as a school counselor, once a source of pride, is now a source of daily terror. The ordinary stress of a challenging student case feels unbearable, a trigger that floods him with the appraisal that he is going to fail this child, too. The resulting fear is a physical force, a tightness in his chest that feels so real it seems to pull the memory of the accident right to the surface. To escape the feeling, he retreats into administrative tasks, letting student emails go unanswered. At home, his wife’s suggestion that he schedule a routine physical sent a jolt of panic through him—the thought of any medical procedure brought back the image of paramedics working on Leo. He immediately changed the subject, a strategy of avoidance that is now second nature. At night, he lies awake for hours, convinced that he must remain alert, that if he truly relaxes, some other unforeseen catastrophe of his own making will unfold.

David finally sought help after his wife found him standing frozen in the kitchen, staring at the toaster oven where a piece of bread had burned. The acrid smell, so similar to the ozone scent of the saw’s overworked motor, had triggered a full sensory reliving of the accident. He was there, in the yard, but also in his kitchen, unable to move or speak. He knows what happened, but when he tries to explain these moments to his wife, he is unable to find the words, a silent testament to the horror. It was in the aftermath of this episode, seeing the fear in his wife’s eyes, that he realized his attempts to contain the damage were destroying everything he cared about. He came to therapy holding onto a fragile hope that he might one day be able to forgive himself, but terrified of the deeper truth he carries: that he is unforgivable, and that he can never trust himself again.
